**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** [Supervising Partner]
**From:** [Associate]
**Re:** Mouloul Energy Materials, Inc. / Acquisition of Kessrin Cell Recovery, Inc.: Review of Execution Set
**Client:** Mouloul Energy Materials, Inc. (Buyer)

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed all seven documents in the folder:

1. Stock Purchase Agreement dated as of May 11, 2026 (the "SPA"), execution version, purchase price $86,400,000.
2. Form of Bill of Sale (SPA Exhibit A).
3. Form of IP Assignment Agreement (SPA Exhibit B).
4. Form of Transition Services Agreement (SPA Exhibit C) (the "TSA").
5. Signed Letter of Intent dated February 9, 2026 (the "LOI").
6. Calder & Fenn insurance certificate cover letter dated May 12, 2026.
7. Landlord estoppel certificate for the Baytown facility dated May 18, 2026.

I found four issues that need correction before signing. Three are high priority.

| # | Issue | Location | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Environmental termination right expires before the SPA is signed | SPA §9.1(e); LOI §6 | **High** |
| 2 | IP Assignment defines "Recycling Process Technology" as patents only, which strips out trade secrets, know-how, process parameters and software | IP Assignment §1.1; SPA §§1.1, 6.6, 11.4 | **High** |
| 3 | TSA chooses Texas law and a Harris County forum, against the SPA's New York law and forum | TSA §12.7; SPA §§11.9, 11.10, 11.4 | **High / Medium** |
| 4 | Seller (as Provider) may assign the TSA to anyone, including a competitor, without consent | TSA §12.3 | **Medium / High** |

One structural point runs through Issues 2 and 3. **SPA Section 11.4 (Order of Precedence)** provides that "[t]his Agreement controls, except that each Ancillary Agreement controls as to its own subject matter." The Ancillary Agreements include the Bill of Sale, the IP Assignment Agreement and the TSA. Where an ancillary agreement conflicts with the SPA on its own subject matter, **the ancillary agreement wins**. For that reason the conflicts below are not drafting nits that the SPA would cure. As drafted, the narrower or less favorable ancillary terms would govern.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Environmental termination window expires before signing

**Where it appears:** SPA Section 9.1(e); compare LOI Section 6(b) and 6(c).

**What the documents say:**
- SPA §9.1(e) lets Buyer terminate if the Phase II Assessment reports estimated Remediation Costs above **$1,500,000**. Buyer must deliver written notice, with the Phase II report, "no later than **forty-five (45) days after the date of the Letter of Intent**."
- The LOI is dated **February 9, 2026**. Forty-five days after that date is **March 26, 2026**.
- The SPA is dated **May 11, 2026**. The termination window therefore **closed about six weeks before the SPA is signed**.
- LOI §6(b) gives Buyer "an environmental review period of **30 days following execution** of the definitive stock purchase agreement." LOI §6(c) provides that the termination notice is "to be delivered no later than **thirty (30) days following execution of the Definitive Agreement**." Both parties signed the LOI.

**Why it matters to Mouloul:** As drafted, Buyer would sign with **no usable environmental walk-away right**. The right is dead on arrival. Buyer could not exercise it on May 11, 2026 or at any time afterward. This matters for this business. The Facility handles electrolyte solvents, LiPF₆, heavy metals, process liquors, leach residues and black mass, all of which the SPA defines as Hazardous Materials. SPA §6.2 contemplates soil, groundwater and process-area sampling after signing. If that sampling reveals contamination above $1.5 million, Buyer's only protections would be:
- the Section 4.9 environmental representation, which is subject to Disclosure Schedule exceptions; and
- the Section 8.2(d) pre-Closing Release indemnity, which is exposed to the cap and escrow mechanics in Article 8 and to collection risk against Seller.

None of these gives Buyer the right to decline to close. The drafting also departs from the agreed commercial position in LOI §6. That position is non-binding under LOI §12, but it was signed by both parties, and it gives us strong grounds to insist on the correction.

**Recommended fix:** Redraft §9.1(e) to measure the window from signing, consistent with LOI §6:

> "(e) by Buyer, if the Phase II Assessment reports estimated Remediation Costs exceeding $1,500,000, by written notice to Seller, accompanied by a copy of the Phase II Assessment report, delivered no later than thirty (30) days after the date of this Agreement."

I also recommend the following related changes:
- Delete the now-unnecessary reference to the "Letter of Intent" in this section. If the term is not used elsewhere, delete the definition too.
- Consider language under which, if Seller's failure to provide access or cooperation under §6.2 delays the Phase II Assessment, the 30-day period is extended day-for-day.
- Consider a closing condition in §7.2 that Buyer has not delivered a termination notice under §9.1(e) and that the period has expired or been waived. This makes the mechanics consistent.

---

### Issue 2: IP Assignment conveys only patents; trade secrets, know-how, process parameters and software stay with Seller

**Where it appears:** IP Assignment Agreement Section 1.1; compare SPA Section 1.1 (definition), Section 6.6 (assignment covenant) and Section 11.4 (precedence).

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA §1.1:** "Recycling Process Technology" means "patents, trade secrets, know-how, process parameters and software used in the Company's hydrometallurgical metal recovery."
- **SPA §6.6:** Seller shall "assign to the Company all Recycling Process Technology owned by Seller or any of its Affiliates." This assignment "shall be made by Seller's execution and delivery of the IP Assignment Agreement."
- **IP Assignment §1.1:** "Recycling Process Technology" means "the Patents listed on Exhibit A." Exhibit A lists six patents and applications covering selective leaching, cobalt/nickel solvent extraction, lithium carbonate precipitation and reductive leaching. Every conveyance, representation and further-assurance provision in the IP Assignment (§§2.1, 4.3, 5.1) runs off that narrow definition.
- **LOI §3(b)** confirms the commercial deal. Seller is to assign "all patents, trade secrets, know-how, process parameters and software."
- **SPA §11.4** makes the IP Assignment Agreement control as to its own subject matter, which is the conveyance of IP.

**Why it matters to Mouloul:** Because of §11.4, the IP Assignment's narrow definition governs what is actually conveyed at Closing. The Company would receive the patents and **would not receive**:
- the leach-chemistry trade secrets and know-how;
- the process parameters (reagent ratios, temperatures, residence times, pH set points, and similar); and
- the process control software.

These unpatented assets are typically the core value of a hydrometallurgical recycling business. Patents disclose the process at a general level. The operating recipe is what makes it economic. Seller would keep title and could use or license that technology. The 5-year non-compete in SPA §6.9 restricts Seller's own recycling activity in North America. It does not stop Seller from licensing the know-how to a third party or using it outside North America.

Buyer's fallback claims are weak:
- A claim that Seller breached §6.6 is undercut by the fact that §6.6 itself says the assignment "shall be made" by delivering the IP Assignment in the agreed form.
- The §4.7 sufficiency representation is subject to the cap and basket in §8.4.
- The IP Assignment §6.1 "no merger" clause preserves SPA remedies. It does not expand the conveyance.

A related point: the TSA (Schedule A, Service 2) has Seller maintaining the process control system and historian after Closing. If Seller still owns the control software, the Company's operational dependence on Seller continues past the 9-month Service Term.

**Recommended fix:** Use both of the following, as belt and braces:
1. **Conform IP Assignment §1.1** to the SPA definition:
   > "'Recycling Process Technology' means all patents (including the Patents listed on Exhibit A), trade secrets, know-how, process parameters, software (in source and object code), and related documentation owned by Assignor or any of its Affiliates and used in, or held for use in, the Company's hydrometallurgical metal recovery."
   
   Add delivery mechanics for non-patent IP: delivery of source code, process documentation, lab notebooks and parameter sets. Add a covenant that Seller will not retain copies, other than what is required by Law, and will keep any retained information confidential.
2. **Amend SPA §11.4** so that the SPA controls in any conflict on the scope of assets conveyed. Alternatively, carve out from the precedence rule the definition of Recycling Process Technology and the governing law and forum provisions in Section 11.9 and Section 11.10.
3. Conform SPA §4.7 and the Disclosure Schedule so that the schedule identifies the material trade secrets and software, and not only patents.

---

### Issue 3: TSA governing law and forum (Texas / Harris County) conflicts with the SPA (New York / New York County)

**Where it appears:** TSA Section 12.7; compare SPA Sections 11.9, 11.10 and 11.4.

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA §11.9:** the SPA "and any Ancillary Agreement" are governed by New York law.
- **SPA §11.10:** exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in **New York County, New York** for any action arising out of or relating to the SPA "**or any Ancillary Agreement**."
- **TSA §12.7:** the TSA is governed by the "**laws of the State of Texas**," with exclusive jurisdiction in "the state and federal courts located in **Harris County, Texas**." Harris County is Seller's home forum. Seller is a Texas LLC, and its laboratory is in Houston.
- The Bill of Sale (§§6.2, 6.3) and the IP Assignment (§§7.4, 7.5) both correctly follow New York law and the SPA §11.10 forum. The TSA is the outlier.
- Under **SPA §11.4**, the TSA controls as to its own subject matter, so the Texas clause would likely prevail for service disputes despite the SPA's express reach to Ancillary Agreements.

**Why it matters to Mouloul:** TSA disputes during the 9-month Service Term are likely to overlap with SPA claims. Examples include:
- EHS compliance support failures (Service 3) that lead to permit issues and environmental indemnity claims;
- accounting support (Service 7) that affects the Closing Working Capital true-up under §2.3; and
- breaches of data confidentiality bearing on the §6.5 confidentiality and §6.9 non-compete covenants.

With conflicting exclusive-forum clauses, Buyer and the Company could face:
- split proceedings in two states under two bodies of law;
- inconsistent results;
- jurisdictional fights over which clause governs a mixed claim; and
- litigating service claims in Seller's home forum.

The TSA's jury waiver (§12.8) and specific-performance clause (§12.9) would also be interpreted under Texas law. The enforceability of pre-dispute jury waivers and the related procedural requirements differ between the two states.

**Recommended fix:** Replace TSA §12.7 with language that tracks the Bill of Sale and IP Assignment:

> "12.7 Governing Law; Jurisdiction. This Agreement is governed by the laws of the State of New York, without regard to conflict of laws principles that would require application of the laws of another jurisdiction. Any action arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall be brought in accordance with Section 11.10 of the Purchase Agreement."

As noted under Issue 2, also amend SPA §11.4 so that §§11.9–11.11 control over any inconsistent ancillary-agreement provision.

---

### Issue 4: Seller may assign the TSA to anyone, including a competitor, without consent

**Where it appears:** TSA Section 12.3.

**What the document says:** "Provider may assign this Agreement, or delegate any of its obligations under it, in whole or in part, to **any Person without the consent of Recipient**." The Recipient (the Company, which Mouloul will own) may not assign without Provider's consent. The SPA's own anti-assignment clause (SPA §11.5) applies only to the SPA and does not reach the TSA.

**Why it matters to Mouloul:**
- **Competitive exposure.** In receiving and performing the Services, the Provider handles "Recipient Data." TSA §1.1 defines this to include plant operating data, process control records, yields, assay results, feedstock supplier lists and terms, black-mass and metal offtake terms, and pricing. Seller could assign or delegate the TSA to a competing battery recycler, which would then gain access to exactly the information that drives the Company's competitive position.
  - The confidentiality covenants (TSA Article 7) and use restrictions (§6.1) would bind the assignee. They are an imperfect remedy once a competitor has seen the data.
  - The SPA §6.9 non-compete binds Seller and its Affiliates only. It does not bind an unaffiliated assignee.
- **Service quality and continuity.** The Services are operationally critical: process control system support, EHS compliance reporting, assay services and feedstock logistics. Free assignment lets Seller hand them to an unknown or under-resourced provider. An assignee with competing interests could also deprioritize the Company. The Service Standard in §2.2 measures performance against Seller's past practice, which a third party may be unable to replicate.
- **Asymmetry.** The Company cannot assign without consent, yet Seller can. This is off-market for a TSA that benefits a buyer.
- **Partial delegation.** "In whole or in part" permits fragmenting the Services across multiple parties, which makes performance and liability harder to manage. §2.3 keeps Provider responsible for subcontractors, but that does not clearly cover an outright assignment.

**Recommended fix:** Replace §12.3 with:

> "12.3 Assignment. Neither party may assign this Agreement, or delegate any of its obligations under it, in whole or in part, without the prior written consent of the other party, except that Recipient may assign this Agreement without consent to Buyer or any Affiliate of Buyer, or to any successor to all or substantially all of the Business. Any purported assignment or delegation in violation of this Section 12.3 is void. Any permitted subcontracting by Provider does not relieve Provider of its obligations, and Provider remains responsible for its subcontractors under Section 2.3."

Do not include any exception that allows Provider to transfer to a competitor of the Company. If Seller insists on flexibility for internal reorganizations, limit any carve-out to a controlled Affiliate of Seller that:
- is bound by SPA §6.9;
- assumes all obligations in writing; and
- leaves Seller jointly and severally liable.

---

## III. Other Documents Reviewed: No Action Items

- **Bill of Sale (Exhibit A):** Consistent with SPA §§1.1 and 6.7. It follows New York law and the SPA forum (§§6.2–6.3), and properly excludes IP, which goes through the IP Assignment (§3.2). Schedule 1 model and serial numbers are still bracketed and must be completed before Closing.
- **Insurance certificate cover letter (Calder & Fenn, May 12, 2026):** Background closing item. It confirms that occurrence-based policies, including site-specific pollution legal liability, are in force through January 1, 2027, consistent with SPA §6.10. It creates no rights (§2.1), and Mouloul is not an additional insured (§2.3). No conflict with the transaction documents. We may wish to follow up separately on the loss runs (§4.1) and post-Closing access to the pollution policy for pre-Closing occurrences.
- **Landlord estoppel (Gulfline, May 18, 2026):** Supports the SPA §7.2(d) condition. It confirms the Lease is in full force, there are no defaults, recycling and hydrometallurgical operations are a permitted use (§2.9), there are no environmental notices (§2.10), and the landlord consents to the change of control (§3.1). No conflict with the transaction documents.

---

## IV. Points I Cannot Resolve from the Documents

1. **Signing status and timing.** The SPA is marked "Execution Version" and dated as of May 11, 2026, and the signature blocks are blank. However, the insurance letter (May 12) and the estoppel (May 18) both describe the SPA as already entered into. Please confirm whether the SPA has been signed.
   - If it has not, the fixes above can go into the execution draft.
   - If it has, Issues 1–4 require a written amendment signed by both parties under SPA §11.3. For Issue 1, we would need Seller to agree to a fresh 30-day window running from the amendment date.
   - The §9.1(b) outside date of **September 30, 2026** has also passed. If Closing has not occurred, we should confirm whether it was extended.
2. **Phase II status.** I cannot tell from the file whether the Phase II Assessment has been commissioned or completed, or what Remediation Costs it estimates. This determines how much Issue 1 matters in practice, and whether a 30-day post-signing window is long enough for sampling and reporting.
3. **Scope of unpatented technology and ownership.** The documents do not identify the specific trade secrets, process parameters or software, or which Seller entity holds them. Exhibit A to the IP Assignment and Disclosure Schedule §4.7 are not in the folder in completed form, and the patent numbers are bracketed. We should get a schedule of the non-patent technology and confirm whether any of it is licensed in from third parties. Third-party licensed technology may need consents to transfer, which IP Assignment §5.1(b) would otherwise contradict.
4. **Service Fees and performance metrics.** TSA Schedule A fees are bracketed, and metrics are left to post-Closing agreement. I cannot assess whether "at cost" pricing is accurate. I also cannot tell whether any Service depends on third-party consents (TSA §2.5) that are not yet in hand.
5. **Whether Seller owns or plans to own a competing business.** This is relevant to how hard to press Issue 4. We should ask the client about Seller's and Halvorsen's other activities in the sector.

Please let me know if you would like me to prepare a markup of the SPA, IP Assignment and TSA reflecting these changes, together with a short issues list for Seller's counsel.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Supervising Partner]
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 17, 2026
**Re:** Mouloul Energy Materials, Inc. / Kessrin Cell Recovery, Inc.: review of execution set

---

## I. Summary

Mouloul Energy Materials, Inc. ("**Buyer**") is buying all outstanding shares of Kessrin Cell Recovery, Inc. (the "**Company**") from Porert Industrial Holdings, LLC ("**Seller**") for $86,400,000 (SPA §2.1). I reviewed all seven documents in the folder:

1. Stock Purchase Agreement dated as of May 11, 2026 (the "**SPA**")
2. Form of Bill of Sale (SPA Ex. A)
3. Form of IP Assignment Agreement (SPA Ex. B)
4. Form of Transition Services Agreement (SPA Ex. C) (the "**TSA**")
5. Letter of Intent dated February 9, 2026 (the "**LOI**")
6. Calder & Fenn insurance certificate cover letter dated May 12, 2026
7. Landlord estoppel certificate (Baytown facility) dated May 18, 2026

I found three substantive issues that need correction before signing:

| # | Issue | Location | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The environmental termination window expired before the SPA date | SPA §9.1(e); LOI §6 | High |
| 2 | The IP Assignment Agreement's patents-only definition of "Recycling Process Technology" controls and strips out trade secrets, know-how and software | IP Assignment §1.1; SPA §§1.1, 6.6, 11.4 | High |
| 3 | Seller, as Provider, may assign the TSA to anyone, including a competitor, without consent | TSA §12.3 | Medium–High |

**Precedence point that affects the analysis.** SPA §11.4 provides that "[t]his Agreement controls, except that each Ancillary Agreement controls as to its own subject matter." "Ancillary Agreements" include the Bill of Sale, the IP Assignment Agreement and the TSA (SPA §1.1). Conflicts between the SPA and an exhibit therefore will **not** be resolved in Buyer's favor by default. On its own subject matter, the exhibit wins.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Environmental termination right expires before signing

**Where:** SPA §9.1(e), read with the LOI date line and LOI §6(b)–(c).

**What the documents say.** SPA §9.1(e) lets Buyer terminate if the Phase II Assessment reports estimated Remediation Costs above $1,500,000. Buyer must deliver written notice, with the Phase II report, "no later than forty-five (45) days after the date of the Letter of Intent." The LOI is dated February 9, 2026. Forty-five days from February 9, 2026 is **March 26, 2026**. The SPA is dated as of **May 11, 2026**, about six weeks after that.

**Why it matters to Buyer.**
- On the day the SPA is signed, the §9.1(e) right has already lapsed. Buyer would sign with **no usable environmental walk-away right**.
- This is a significant gap for this business. The Facility handles electrolyte solvents, LiPF₆, heavy metals, leach liquors and black mass. The Phase II Assessment, which SPA §6.2 contemplates being run after signing, is the main tool for pricing that exposure before Buyer is committed.
- The SPA also departs from the deal both parties signed. LOI §6(b) gives Buyer "an environmental review period of 30 days following execution of the definitive stock purchase agreement." LOI §6(c) states that the termination notice is to be delivered "no later than thirty (30) days following execution of the Definitive Agreement." This looks like a drafting error, not a negotiated concession, which supports asking Seller to fix it.
- The other remedies are not a substitute. The §8.2(d) pre-Closing Release indemnity and the §4.9 rep (5-year survival) are subject to the §8.4 basket and cap and to the escrow mechanics. They give Buyer a damages claim after Closing, not the right to walk away before Closing.

**Recommended fix.** Revise the second sentence of §9.1(e) to read:
> "To exercise this right, Buyer must deliver written notice to Seller, accompanied by a copy of the Phase II Assessment report, no later than thirty (30) days after the date of this Agreement."

Also consider:
- adding a tolling or extension mechanism if Seller's cooperation under §6.2 delays the consultant, for example extending the deadline day-for-day for any delay in site access; and
- adding a corresponding closing condition, so that Buyer is protected if the Phase II report is delivered late in the window.

---

### Issue 2: IP Assignment Agreement's patents-only definition of "Recycling Process Technology" controls

**Where:** IP Assignment Agreement §1.1, conflicting with SPA §1.1 (definition) and SPA §6.6 (assignment covenant), with SPA §11.4 deciding which one prevails.

**What the documents say.**
- **SPA §1.1:** "Recycling Process Technology" means "patents, trade secrets, know-how, process parameters and software used in the Company's hydrometallurgical metal recovery."
- **SPA §6.6:** Seller shall "assign to the Company all Recycling Process Technology owned by Seller or any of its Affiliates … by Seller's execution and delivery of the IP Assignment Agreement."
- **IP Assignment §1.1:** "Recycling Process Technology" means "the Patents listed on Exhibit A." The Patents are the six patents and applications on Exhibit A, with their families.
- **SPA §11.4:** each Ancillary Agreement controls "as to its own subject matter." What is conveyed is the subject matter of the IP Assignment Agreement, so its narrower definition governs.

**Why it matters to Buyer.**
- At Closing the Company would receive only the six listed patent assets. Seller would keep the **trade secrets, know-how, process parameters and software**: the leach chemistry operating parameters, solvent-extraction and precipitation recipes, and process-control software. These are probably the core value of a hydrometallurgical recycler, and much of that value sits outside any patent.
- Seller would remain free to use or license those retained assets. The SPA §6.9 non-compete binds Seller and its Affiliates, but it does not stop Seller from licensing the retained technology to a third-party recycler.
- The SPA's own reps assume the broad scope. SPA §4.7 represents that "the Recycling Process Technology, together with the intellectual property owned by the Company, constitutes all intellectual property necessary to conduct the Business." Seller could argue that the rep, too, should be read against what was actually conveyed. At best, Buyer is left with an indemnity claim, subject to the §8.4 cap of $8,640,000, for an asset that should simply have been transferred.
- No other document fills the gap. Bill of Sale §3.2 states that it conveys no intellectual property. IP Assignment §6.1 (no merger) preserves the SPA covenants as contract claims, but it does not itself convey anything.
- The broad scope is also what the parties agreed. LOI §3(b) calls for assignment of "all patents, trade secrets, know-how, process parameters and software."

**Recommended fix.**
1. Replace IP Assignment §1.1 with the SPA definition, or delete it and rely on IP Assignment §1.3, so that the term "has the meaning given in the Purchase Agreement." Keep "Patents" as a separate, subsidiary defined term for recordation purposes (§§3.1–3.3).
2. Conform §2.1(b) and the §5.1 reps so they cover all Recycling Process Technology, not only Patents. Add delivery mechanics for non-registered items: source code, process documentation, parameter sets and lab notebooks, delivered within a fixed period, by analogy to §4.3.
3. As a backstop, revise SPA §11.4 so that, for the scope of assets to be conveyed under §§6.6 and 6.7, the SPA controls over the Ancillary Agreements.
4. Confirm that SPA Disclosure Schedule §4.7 and IP Assignment Exhibit A list the same patents.

---

### Issue 3: TSA lets Seller assign freely, including to a competitor

**Where:** TSA §12.3.

**What the document says.** "Provider may assign this Agreement, or delegate any of its obligations under it, in whole or in part, to any Person without the consent of Recipient." The Recipient, which is the Company and will be Buyer's subsidiary, may not assign without Provider's consent.

**Why it matters to Buyer.**
- **Competitive exposure.** Seller could assign or delegate services to a competing battery recycler. In performing the services, that assignee would receive "Recipient Data" (TSA §1.1): plant operating data, process control records, yields, assay results, feedstock supplier lists and terms, and black-mass and metal offtake terms and pricing. The Article 7 confidentiality and §6.1 use restriction would bind the assignee, but enforcement after the fact is a weak protection once a competitor has seen the data. Services 2 (process control system support) and 4 (laboratory and assay) involve especially sensitive information.
- **Service continuity and quality.** The TSA covers essential functions for nine months after Closing (TSA §3.1): ERP and IT, DCS support, EHS compliance reporting, assay, hazardous-materials logistics, payroll and accounting. An unvetted assignee could degrade performance. A partial delegation could also split services among several parties and complicate the §2.2 Service Standard, which is tied to how *Provider* performed before Closing.
- **The SPA does not fill the gap.** SPA §11.5 restricts assignment of the SPA only. The SPA §6.9 non-compete restricts Seller's own competitive activity, but it does not clearly prevent Seller from handing the TSA to a third-party competitor.
- **The clause is one-sided.** Recipient needs Provider's consent to assign, but Provider needs nothing.

**Recommended fix.** Replace §12.3 with a mutual consent requirement, along these lines:
> "Neither party may assign this Agreement, or delegate any of its obligations under it, in whole or in part, without the prior written consent of the other party, provided that Recipient may assign this Agreement without consent to Buyer or any Affiliate of Buyer, or to any successor to all or substantially all of the Business. Any purported assignment or delegation in violation of this Section 12.3 is void."

Also:
- do not include any exception for transfers to Seller's successors that could reach a competitor;
- allow subcontracting by Provider only to subcontractors that Recipient approves in advance, with Provider remaining liable (building on §2.3); and
- make clear that the subcontracting carve-out never extends to a Person engaged in lithium-ion battery recycling or black-mass processing.

---

## III. Other documents reviewed

- **Bill of Sale (Ex. A).** No issues found. It conveys the Shredding Line Assets free and clear, delivers them in place, expressly excludes IP (pointing to the IP Assignment), and preserves SPA remedies (§4.2). Schedule 1 serial and model numbers are blank. These should be completed before Closing.
- **Insurance certificate cover letter.** I treated this as a closing-folder item rather than a transaction document. Note that Buyer is listed only as certificate holder, not as additional insured or loss payee (§2.3), and that loss runs are still outstanding (§4.1). It raises no conflict with the SPA. For diligence, it is useful that a site-specific pollution legal liability policy is in place.
- **Landlord estoppel certificate.** I treated this as a closing-folder item. It appears to satisfy the SPA §7.2(d) landlord consent and estoppel condition: it consents to the change of control (§3.1), certifies no defaults, and confirms that the battery recycling and hydrometallurgical uses are permitted. It raises no conflict with the SPA.

---

## IV. Items I could not resolve from the documents

1. **Execution status.** The SPA is marked "Execution Version" and dated as of May 11, 2026, but the signature blocks in our copy are blank. The insurance letter (May 12) and estoppel (May 18) both describe the SPA as already entered into. Please confirm whether the SPA has been signed.
   - If it has not, Issue 1 can be fixed in the document.
   - If it has, §9.1(e) would require a written amendment under §11.3. In the meantime we would need to consider whether the LOI §6 terms help at all. They likely do not, because LOI §12 makes §6 non-binding and LOI §14(a) terminates the LOI on execution of the Definitive Agreement.
2. **Phase II status.** I have no information on whether the Phase II Assessment has been commissioned or what it shows. That determines how important the Issue 1 fix is in practice.
3. **Ownership of unregistered technology.** The documents do not identify which entity actually holds the trade secrets, parameters and software: Seller, an Affiliate or the Company. Before closing we should get a schedule of those assets and their holders, so that SPA §6.6 and IP Assignment §2.2 reach every holder.
4. **TSA Schedule A fees** are blank. We cannot confirm the at-cost pricing in LOI §4 until they are filled in.
5. **Disclosure Schedule** (including §§4.3, 4.6, 4.7) is not in the folder. I could not check the patent list against IP Assignment Exhibit A, or check the consents list.

Please let me know if you would like me to prepare a markup of the SPA, IP Assignment Agreement and TSA reflecting these changes.
